title: Understanding the Curse of Unrolling
claim: A derivative's error can transiently grow before converging, even though the underlying iterate's error decreases steadily.
layout: single log-scale line plot, two curves, dotted vertical line marking peak
description: A single plot with iteration count k on the x-axis (0 to 1000) and error on a log-scale y-axis (about 1e-4 to 1e1). A thin red line shows the iterate error ||x^(k)(u) - x*(u)||. It starts near 4 and falls steadily and almost linearly in log scale to about 1e-3. A thicker green line shows the derivative error ||Dx^(k)(u) - Dx*(u)||. It starts near 8e-3, rises to a peak of about 2.6e-2 near k=110, then declines in parallel with the red line to about 2e-4. A dotted green vertical line marks the peak and is labeled k-dot in the legend. The legend sits in the top right, and grey gridlines cover the plot. The eye goes first to the green hump below the red line.
caption: Iterate $\xk (\u)$ vs derivative $\deriv \xk (\u)$ error plot for gradient descent applied to $f (\x, u) \coloneqq \norm{A\x - \b}^2/2 + u\norm{\x}^2/2$. Unlike $\xk (\u)$, $\deriv\xk (\u)$ initially drifts away from its limit before eventually coming back to it. We provide a non-asymptotic understanding of this transient behavior, called the curse of unrolling, and study simple ways to mitigate it.
abstract: Algorithm unrolling is ubiquitous in machine learning, particularly in hyperparameter optimization and meta-learning, where Jacobians of solution mappings are computed by differentiating through iterative algorithms. Although unrolling is known to yield asymptotically correct Jacobians under suitable conditions, recent work has shown that the derivative iterates may initially diverge from the true Jacobian, a phenomenon known as the curse of unrolling. In this work, we provide a non-asymptotic analysis that explains the origin of this behavior and identifies the algorithmic factors that govern it. We show that truncating early iterations of the derivative computation mitigates the curse while simultaneously reducing memory requirements. Finally, we demonstrate that warm-starting in bilevel optimization naturally induces an implicit form of truncation, providing a practical remedy. Our theoretical findings are supported by numerical experiments on representative examples.
